title: Baptism
hookLine: water poured three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit

cards: Sunday afternoon, at the back of a church. A baby in a white outfit that took three people to get onto her. Grandparents with phones up.
A godmother holding a candle a little too close to her hair.

The priest takes a small shell or a jug and pours water over the baby's forehead, once, twice, three times, saying the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The baby is often furious about it.
Everyone else is smiling. Catholics believe something enormous just happened, in a few seconds. The first of the seven: baptism.

teach.b: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, plunge or immerse. Some churches go right under the water; others pour, and the Catholic Church allows both. Either way, the sign is washing: going under, coming up.
Jesus himself was baptized by John in the Jordan.

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON, SPIRIT.
teach.b: At the end of Matthew's Gospel he sends his followers out with this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
That's where the three names come from, and the three pourings follow them.

teach.h: A NEW BIRTH, ONCE, FOR GOOD.
teach.b: The Catechism names what Catholics believe it does: sins washed away, a new birth as a child of God, membership in the Church, and a mark on the soul that can never be undone, which is why a person is baptized only once.

In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit. So Catholics call it a birth; some keep the date like a birthday. No baby comes alone.
Godparents promise to help raise the child in the faith. In many Hispanic families they're padrinos, and the parents and godparents become compadres, family for life.
In many Filipino families they're ninong and ninang, and there are often several. Two surprises.

teach.h: ANYONE CAN BAPTIZE IN AN EMERGENCY.
teach.b: In an emergency, anyone can baptize, even someone who isn't Christian, pouring water and saying those words, intending what the Church does.

teach.h: BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: And the Church recognizes other Christian churches' baptisms done with water and the same three names.
Christians differ on when: Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and others baptize babies, while Baptists and others baptize only those old enough to profess faith.

how: Catholics are usually baptized as babies: the priest or deacon pours water over the head three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with godparents promising to help raise the child in the faith.

o: a yearly blessing with water for good health
a washing in water Catholics see as a new birth
a naming ceremony that welcomes a new baby

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: only a priest can ever baptize
in an emergency, anyone can, even someone who isn't Christian, using water and the words.
the Church teaches baptism leaves a mark that can never be undone.
Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Anglicans do; Baptists and others baptize only those who profess faith.

games.q: Jesus is sending his followers out for the last time in Matthew's Gospel. what does he tell them to do?
o: teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost.
games.why: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." the three names at every font come from here.

practice: If you were baptized, think of who was there: who held you, who promised things for you. If you weren't, think of a baptism you've seen, or simply of water, the first splash of a morning shower, rain on your face.
If you pray, thank God for the people who carried you.

wordCard.voice: Baptism. From the Greek for dipping under. Water in the three names and, Catholics believe, a second birth. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to dip, plunge or immerse.

carryVoice: Your line: your first birthday. Water, three names, a new birth. That's day one hundred twenty-six.
